Picomatch



Blazing fast and accurate glob matcher written in JavaScript.
No dependencies and full support for standard and extended Bash glob features, including braces, extglobs, POSIX brackets, and regular expressions.



## Why picomatch? * **Lightweight** - No dependencies * **Minimal** - Tiny API surface. Main export is a function that takes a glob pattern and returns a matcher function. * **Fast** - Loads in about 2ms (that's several times faster than a [single frame of a HD movie](http://www.endmemo.com/sconvert/framespersecondframespermillisecond.php) at 60fps) * **Performant** - Use the returned matcher function to speed up repeat matching (like when watching files) * **Accurate matching** - Using wildcards (`*` and `?`), globstars (`**`) for nested directories, [advanced globbing](#advanced-globbing) with extglobs, braces, and POSIX brackets, and support for escaping special characters with `\` or quotes. * **Well tested** - Thousands of unit tests See the [library comparison](#library-comparisons) to other libraries.

candidates.readme_excerpt:
# tinyasr

**Tiny** **A**utomatic **S**peech **R**ecognition library for running new trained Zipformer2 models, aimed to bring accurate on device speech recognition with small to download models.

Demo at: https://dkaraush.github.io/tinyasr/web/

- Small multilingual [models](#models), benchmarked on FLEURS and Common Voice.
- RNN-T and TDT transducers, stateless or LSTM-hybrid decoders; greedy or beam search (width 4 by default).
- Punctuation, capitalization and word timestamps.
- Live streaming with re-decodes of the open sentence, or a full-context pass over a finished recording.
- Built-in Silero VAD and end-of-turn head: knows when the speaker has finished a sentence.
- SIMD on ARM (`i8mm`, `dotprod` or plain NEON, picked at runtime), x86_64 SSE, and WASM; int4 weights stay int4 in memory (~46 MB loaded for a 38 MB model).
- Multi-threading supported.
- Zero dependencies.

### Building (Native)

```bash
cargo build --release --features c-api
# library will be built at target/release/libtinyasr.a
# include headers are at include/tinyasr.h
```

### Models

candidates.readme_excerpt:
# caramel, a conversation model trained *only* on speech
*10 November 2026*

Model: [huggingface.co/naklecha/caramel-1](https://huggingface.co/naklecha/caramel-1)

I trained a speech-to-speech model inspired by [Dessa](https://block.xyz/dessa). I'm calling the model `caramel-1`. The model learned from recordings of people talking and nothing else, and **has never seen a single word of text**. The code, the training recipe and the weights are open source.

`caramel-1` sounds incredibly human. Most of what `caramel-1` says doesn't make sense yet, but the sentences make a little more sense every time I add more data.

**Two copies of the same model can talk to each other in real time**. Every 80 ms, each copy listens to the other and decides whether to speak or stay quiet. `caramel-1` generates audio about 11 times faster than real time on a GPU, so it's fast enough to talk to a person live. It even keeps up on my MacBook Pro (M3 Pro), where both copies together run about 4 times faster than real time.

[![two copies of caramel-1 talking, with live transcripts](docs/cover.png)](https://naklecha.com/research/caramel-1)
*Watch and listen to the samples at [naklecha.com/research/caramel-1](https://naklecha.com/research/caramel-1). Two copies of `caramel-1` talk to each other in real time; the transcripts come from a speech recogniser and are only there so you can follow along.*

**[▶ Watch all sixteen samples in one video](https://github.com/naklecha/caramel/blob/main/docs/caramel_samples.mp4)** (16 minutes).

## scoring conversations
I started by measuring Dessa's example conversations. I measured 13 statistics on them and turned each one into a target band. Most of the statistics are about timing, like how much people overlap, how long the gaps between turns are and how many backchannels (the "mm-hm"s people make while someone else talks) there are per minute. The rest are about the recording, like cross-talk between the two tracks and the noise floor. A conversation's closeness score is how far its statistics sit outside those bands, averaged, so **0 means the conversation looks like Dessa on every statistic**.

I also ran the score on conversations I broke on purpose, to make sure it catches bad ones. # airdrop-agent

**A local operator for the work that happens before a token exists.** Identities, wallets, social
accounts, quests, testnets and waitlists — driven by one CLI and one policy engine, with an MCP
surface for other agents.

No server. No telemetry. SQLite plus an encrypted vault in `~/.airdrop-agent`.

```
aa quest probe https://app.example.com/points   # read the page, don't guess
aa quest run dow-points --identity main        # run it inside policy
aa cf assist --identity main                   # one visible click when a challenge wins
aa autopilot tick                              # radar → warm → daily → quests → faucet
```

> New in 4.1 — clearance stored per host and user agent, one persistent browser profile per identity,
> encrypted session restore, quest login pre-flight, nineteen tested targets. Full manual:
> [docs/GUIDE.md](docs/GUIDE.md). New here? Read [docs/INTRO.md](docs/INTRO.md).

## What an airdrop agent is

Airdrops pay after the fact. You use a testnet, hold points, fill a waitlist, keep a streak for
months — and a snapshot decides later whether any of it was worth anything. The work is repetitive,
time-windowed, spread over many accounts, and easy to get wrong at the exact moment it matters: one
wrong signature and a wallet is empty.

An airdrop agent is the operations layer for that work. Not a macro that clicks one button — a
system that holds the whole loop:

| layer | question it answers |
|---|---|
| identity graph | who is acting:

# pstack [![Buy Me A Coffee](https://img.shields.io/badge/Buy%20Me%20A%20Coffee-support-yellow?logo=buy-me-a-coffee&logoColor=white)](https://buymeacoffee.com/codenyer) [![Mentioned in Awesome Claude Code](https://awesome.re/mentioned-badge.svg)](https://github.com/hesreallyhim/awesome-claude-code) Lauren Tan's [pstack](https://github.com/cursor/plugins/tree/main/pstack) is an opinionated Cursor skill stack that improves agent outcomes. This is a port for Claude Code, Codex, Pi, GitHub Copilot, Muse, and other agent harnesses. It tracks upstream and also carries named policy forks, each declared in [`tools/forks.json`](tools/forks.json). Tell `poteto-mode` your goal and it will invoke the correct workflow for the task. It keeps your code concise, simple and verified. For concurrency bugs and invariants that tests cannot reach, `/create-formal-verification-skill` picks the riskiest property in your code, verifies it with a tool that fits, and leaves a project skill the next agent reruns. The separate [agent-formal-verify](https://github.com/michael-denyer/agent-formal-verify) plugin goes deeper on the method, with guided TLA+ model checking, Lean proofs, and Kani for Rust. ## Built for Claude Code This port translates upstream's Cursor skills for Claude Code before installation. [Upstream's Claude Code install](https://github.com/cursor/plugins/tree/2f87c85/harness/pstack/claude-code) asks agents to translate Cursor names at runtime, using extra tokens and relying on them to apply the mapping correctly. This port also adds a SessionStart hook that routes tasks to `poteto-mode`. ## Install
Claude Code Run in Claude Code 2.1.292 or later: ```text /plugin marketplace add michael-denyer/pstack-claude /plugin install pstack@pstack-claude ``` Claude Code leaves auto-update off for third-party marketplaces, so pstack stays on the version you installed. To turn it on, run `/plugin`, open the **Marketplaces** tab, select `pstack-claude`, and choose **Enable auto-update**. To update once by hand, run `claude plugin update pstack@pstack-claude`.
Codex Run in your terminal: ```shell codex plugin marketplace add michael-denyer/pstack-claude codex plugin add pstack@pstack-claude ``` Invoke a skill by typing `$` and its name, such as `$poteto-mode` or `$babysit`, then choosing its entry, which inserts `$pstack:`. `/skills` lists e
